In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of CD4 T cells in immunity to infection.

understanding the mechanisms that control the development, differentiation and function of T lymphocytes, with a focus on how the immune system responds to infection and how this response can be manipulated to treat human disease.
the mechanisms by which the immune system controls the development of CD4+ helper T cells (TH), and how TH cells are regulated by the innate immune system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the authors have shown a novel mechanism by which TLR9 and CD8α+ DC sensing of self-DNA controls cell-mediated immunity to listeria infection via the rapid conversion of conventional CD4+ T cells to Treg.
Listeria infection can be controlled by CD4+ T cells in a dose-dependent manner: a low dose of Listeria induces a TH cell response and a high dose induces a Treg cell response.
Listeria infection can induce the rapid conversion of conventional CD4+ T cells to immunosupressive Treg.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CD4+ T cells are plastic and can rapidly be converted into Treg in response to infection.
CD4+ T cells are able to be converted from TH cells to Treg cells during infection.
CD4+ T cells can be rapidly converted to immunosuppresive regulatory T cells (Treg).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the innate immune system is able to rapidly reprogram the adaptive immune system.
the innate immune system can rapidly convert CD4+ T helper cells to T regulatory cells in response to infection.
the same pathogen, Listeria, can induce either a TH or Treg response depending on the size or the dose of the initial inoculum.
